entry.title: Toward Dexterous Mobile Manipulation
entry.content:
Speaker: Nikolaus Correll, University of Notre Dame
Date: October 30, 2026
Series: Purdue ICON Weekly Seminar

The talk examined what is still required to make dexterous mobile manipulation useful outside a demonstration. Correll connected earlier industrial manipulation systems with current work on EV battery disassembly, humanoid control, and simulation-based optimization. A recurring theme was choosing where to use learned capabilities and where established robotics methods already provide useful tools.

The available recording begins during an example and ends partway through the final discussion. These notes summarize that recording, supported by three screenshots from the presentation.

A working demonstration is only part of the application

The opening examples covered industrial kitting and assembly, gentle handling of strawberries, grocery picking, and integration with a worker’s task-tracking interface. They illustrated capabilities that could be achieved with relatively structured systems, including wrist-mounted vision and independently controlled gripper fingers.

They also exposed limitations that a short video can hide. A shelf-restocking demonstration may cover only a small reachable area, while a complete application requires access to other heights and locations. A successful manipulation skill still needs to fit the surrounding workflow and solve a problem that an industrial partner is willing to adopt.

In one strawberry-handling example, regulating motor current was sufficient without using the available tactile sensors. Later examples returned to the benefits of fingertip sensing. The role of sensing therefore depended on the task and the mechanical system being controlled.

Use battery disassembly as a concrete target

EV battery disassembly provided the main application for the current work. The proposed workflow combines industrial robots, additional manipulation capabilities, and human work at selected stages. The aim is to reduce difficult manual handling while retaining as much conventional automation as practical.

One prototype paired a trained detector for battery-specific components with a registered representation of the battery’s geometry and parts. A language interface could then interpret a request such as removing the remaining screws and connect it to the corresponding objects and robot actions.

The example made the supporting infrastructure important: the instruction becomes useful because the system has a record of the parts, their locations, and the available operations. Extending the workflow to picking up loosened screws, changing tools, or removing other components adds further manipulation problems.

Combine high-level reasoning with existing robot tools

The architecture described in the talk combined language and vision models with simulation, perception, navigation, control, and memory. Correll argued for retaining established methods for tasks such as localization and navigation rather than expecting one foundation model to relearn the entire robotics stack.

A persistent challenge is representing what the robot has seen and how the scene changes after an action. A useful memory needs to track objects and their locations while allowing updates when a screw is removed, a part moves, or the robot changes viewpoint.

This places language-based interaction within a larger system. The high-level request still has to connect to an executable skill, current state information, and a controller suited to the hardware.

Manipulation and balance cannot be separated

A humanoid that can walk or wave does not automatically provide the control needed for manipulation. Forces at the wrists affect the rest of the body, while a balancing response that takes a step can interfere with a precise arm task.

One approach fed an encoding of wrist forces into a learned lower-body policy. The goal was to make the robot account for manipulation loads while maintaining its stance. The talk presented this as continuing work rather than a completed solution to whole-body manipulation.

Correll also discussed model predictive control using physics simulation and derivatives of simulated quantities. A task can be expressed through costs on virtual sensor outputs, allowing numerical optimization to search for useful actions. Examples included standing, responding to disturbances, and leaning against a work surface.

The experiments showed both opportunities and limitations. Online optimization could produce useful behaviour without training a new policy for every example, but local minima and recovery failures remained problems. Reinforcement learning performed better in some of the comparisons shown. The discussion therefore treated optimization and learning as complementary tools whose roles depend on the task.

Dexterity also depends on hand geometry

Another theme was that a hand’s appearance does not establish its manipulation capability. Limited finger and thumb motions can force substantial changes in wrist orientation or body posture to grasp objects of different sizes. Computing a grasp then involves more than deciding how far to close the fingers.

The examples used simulation-based optimization to account for those geometric constraints. A separate contact experiment compared force measurements at the wrist and fingers, motivating sensing closer to the interaction when a local contact signal is needed to trigger a reflex.

The talk also explored using language models to suggest approximate physical properties, including mass, friction, and stiffness. These estimates could be combined with simple mechanical relationships, such as a spring model, to choose grasping forces for fragile objects. The role of the model was to provide a useful prior that the robot could connect to physical control.

Precision becomes harder when the base can move

A screw-picking comparison illustrated the gap between a fixed manipulator and mobile manipulation. Correll reported substantially better reliability when the humanoid was supported than when it stood independently, with a further decline in a condition involving locomotion.

The explanation involved body motion, stability, and uncertainty about the target’s location. Visual servoing was already being used, so adding vision alone had not removed the difficulty. The robot still needed accurate coordination between the moving base, hand, and object.

This was one of the talk’s central deployment questions: how can a system preserve the precision of a manipulation skill when the platform supporting that skill is itself moving?

Bring real environments into simulation

The real-to-sim examples constructed simulation assets from observations of physical objects and environments. Once an object or scene is represented in a simulator, a controller can be explored or optimized before trying the behaviour on the robot.

Another example combined human motion tracking with retargeting to a humanoid. This could provide a starting demonstration, followed by simulation-based refinement or the generation of additional training examples. Differences in body size and movement still have to be handled explicitly; a human step does not always correspond to a single robot step.

The talk also noted that a plausible-looking asset may not reproduce the physical behaviour of the object, as in the example of a generated cable model. Obtaining the geometry is therefore useful progress, while contact and dynamics remain part of making the simulation suitable for control.

Toward useful systems

The closing discussion connected these methods to laboratory assistance, lower-cost research platforms, better actuators and sensing, and more integrated mechanical design. In the questions, Correll emphasized that the mechanism itself can eliminate or create major control difficulties.

Safety was another unresolved part of the full system. For example, stopping an action must be considered together with the robot’s balance and contact state. The overall direction was to combine advances in language and vision models with optimization, learning, and established automation around specific applications whose reliability can be tested.

Sources

The Purdue ICON series announcement lists the October 30 talk. The speaker’s Notre Dame faculty page provides his name and affiliation. The summary follows the supplied transcript and screenshots; unclear names and incomplete answers are not reconstructed.
entry.summary: Nikolaus Correll on combining industrial automation, language models, optimization, and robot learning for dexterous mobile manipulation.

entry.title: Statistical Inference with AI-Generated Predictive Distributions

link.title: Statistical Inference with AI-Generated Predictive Distributions

entry.content:
Speaker: Emma Jingfei Zhang, Emory University
Date: October 30, 2026
Series: Purdue Quantitative Methods Seminar

The seminar asked how AI-generated predictions can improve statistical inference without treating them as observed outcomes. The central idea was distribution-informed prediction-powered inference (DiPPI): retain information from a predictive distribution, then use a smaller labeled sample to learn how that information should enter the estimator.

These notes combine the recorded discussion with four slide photos. The recording starts after the introduction and ends during a question; the photos clarify the displayed notation and one application.

Predictions supplement observed outcomes

The setup contains a small labeled sample with covariates $X_i$ and observed responses $Y_i$, together with a larger unlabeled sample where the responses are missing. A pretrained model supplies predictions for both samples.

Simply averaging AI-generated responses can leave systematic prediction bias intact. The role of the labeled observations is to estimate a correction. More generated responses can reduce sampling variability in the predictions, but do not by themselves remove their bias.

For a fixed prediction function $f$, the basic PPI mean estimator combines predictions on the unlabeled sample with residuals from the labeled sample:

\[\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{PPI}} =\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=n+1}^{n+N}f(X_j) +\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(Y_i-f(X_i)\bigr).\]

Here $n$ is the number of labeled observations and $N$ the number of additional unlabeled observations. The slide gave its variance as

\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{PPI}}) =\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y-f(X))}{n} +\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f(X))}{N}.\]

This expression uses independent labeled and unlabeled samples and treats the externally trained predictor as fixed. It does not require the residual $Y-f(X)$ to be independent of $f(X)$ within an observation, a distinction raised in the discussion.

When predictions explain the response well, the residual variance can be much smaller than the response variance. However, an unhelpful prediction function can make the basic estimator less efficient than using only the labeled outcomes.

A distribution can retain information that a point prediction loses

The talk illustrated this with two rating distributions: one puts all its mass at 3, while another puts equal mass at 1 and 5. Both have mean 3, but communicate different uncertainty.

For each observation, DiPPI uses a predictive distribution $Q_i$ rather than only a predicted response. Its spread, shape, or other features may help explain the outcome or the reliability of a prediction. Those features are useful when they carry information relevant to the statistical quantity being estimated.

The setup does not require $Q_i$ to equal the true conditional distribution of $Y_i$. Predictions can be misspecified and can incorporate auxiliary text or image information. The labeled and unlabeled observations must still satisfy the common-population assumptions of the method; the correction is not a general solution to arbitrary population shifts.

Calibrate the estimating function

The target parameter is defined through a population estimating equation,

\[\mathbb{E}\bigl[U_\theta(X,Y)\bigr]=0.\]

For a mean, $U_\theta$ can be $Y-\theta$. For linear regression, it can be $X(Y-X^{\mathsf T}\theta)$. The analyst chooses the target and corresponding estimating function before using AI information to improve its estimation.

The method predicts this estimating function using $h_\theta(X,Q)$. The displayed estimator solves

\[\frac{1}{n+N}\sum_{i=1}^{n+N}h_\theta(X_i,Q_i) +\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\{U_\theta(X_i,Y_i)-h_\theta(X_i,Q_i)\right\} =0.\]

The first term uses predictions on all observations. The second uses labeled observations to correct the prediction. At the population level, the two contributions involving $h_\theta$ cancel, preserving the original estimating equation. The choice of $h_\theta$ determines how much variance can be reduced.

The oracle choice discussed in the talk was

\[h_\theta^\star(X,Q) =\mathbb{E}\bigl[U_\theta(X,Y)\mid X,Q\bigr].\]

This calibrates the quantity defining the parameter using both the covariates and distributional information. In practice, the conditional expectation is unknown and must be estimated. Discrete predictive distributions can be represented by probability vectors; continuous distributions may be represented through summaries or basis coefficients. The information retained in that representation matters for the attainable efficiency.

Cross-fitting and protection against negative learning

The implementation splits labeled data into three parts with separate roles: obtaining a preliminary parameter estimate, fitting the prediction function, and constructing the corrected estimator using held-out labeled data and the unlabeled sample. Rotating the roles produces three estimates that are then combined.

This cross-fitting separates nuisance estimation from the observations used to evaluate its correction. The talk also introduced a calibration matrix that adjusts the strength and direction of the predicted score contribution, reducing reliance on predictions that provide little useful information.

The theoretical discussion distinguished several results. Under the stated regularity and convergence conditions, the cross-fitted estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. The additional calibration provides a positive-learning guarantee relative to labeled-only inference in terms of asymptotic covariance. When the fitted conditional expectation is consistent for the oracle function, the estimator can attain the relevant efficiency bound for the chosen representation.

These are asymptotic statements under assumptions, rather than a promise that every finite-data run improves on every baseline. The confidence-interval slide described a consistent estimate of the asymptotic covariance, which supports the corresponding normal-approximation intervals.

Application: politeness ratings

One example used written requests from Stack Exchange and Wikipedia, together with human politeness ratings and an indicator for hedging language. The target was the coefficient on that indicator in a regression of the human ratings.

The model supplied probabilities over 25 possible rating levels. DiPPI could use this distribution rather than collapse it to a single predicted rating.

The slide compared labeled-only estimation, point-prediction methods, and DiPPI using relative RMSE, confidence-interval width, and empirical coverage across different labeled fractions. The example showed gains in estimation error and interval width for DiPPI; coverage was reported separately and varied across methods and labeled fractions.

Extension: deciding which outcomes to collect

The closing discussion considered a fixed labeling budget. Instead of accepting a predetermined split between labeled and unlabeled observations, an investigator could choose which individuals to survey using their covariates and predictive distributions.

The objective is to select observations that improve inference about the target parameter. The speaker described jointly choosing the sampling strategy and estimating procedure as ongoing work, alongside possible extensions involving multiple predictive distributions.

Sources and further reading

The Purdue QM seminar schedule provides the speaker, title, and date. The summary follows the supplied transcript and slide photos; unclear formula references and unrecorded material are not reconstructed.

Related paper: Maoyu Zhang, Jingfei Zhang, and Xuming He. Beyond Point Predictions: Distribution-Informed Prediction-Powered Inference, 2026.
entry.summary: Using predictive distributions, score calibration, and cross-fitting to improve statistical inference with limited labeled data.

entry.title: Robotics and Embodied AI: From Demos to Deployment

link.title: Robotics and Embodied AI: From Demos to Deployment

entry.content:
Session: Robotics & Embodied AI: Lightning Talks & Panel
Speakers: Yan Gu, Aniket Bera, Zachary Kingston, Rohan Paleja, Shreyas Sundaram, and Raymond Yeh
Moderator: Ananth Grama
Event: Purdue + Google AI Summit 2026
Date: October 29, 2026

This session combined six research presentations with an audience discussion about deploying AI in physical systems. A recurring question was how to connect learned representations and flexible reasoning with the timing, physical constraints, and safety requirements of a robot operating in the real world.

The recording begins during the first presentation and contains several unclear intervals. The summary follows the available material, grouping the discussion by topic.

Physics and adaptation in changing environments

The opening presentation focused on environments that move or change while a robot is acting. Examples included walking on a moving vessel, striking a fast-moving table-tennis ball, and adjusting contact forces when an external disturbance changes the load on an object.

These cases connect physical modelling with adaptive control and learning. A robot cannot assume that its support surface is stationary or that the forces involved in manipulation remain constant. State estimation, prediction, and control need to account for the changing conditions.

Make perception useful to the rest of the system

Another presentation examined the full autonomy pipeline: perception, reasoning, planning, validation, and operation. Many successful systems benefit from carefully prepared environments, such as floor markers, prior maps, or fixed manufacturing procedures. Removing that support exposes harder problems.

The discussion emphasized representations that downstream components can use. A visually convincing reconstruction is not automatically sufficient for a robot that needs a current state estimate, semantic relationships, uncertainty information, and constraints on possible actions.

Examples included constructing useful scene representations from limited visual observations and coordinating heterogeneous robots with different capabilities. The question was how perception can support a checkable decision, rather than simply produce an image or an opaque embedding.

Plan fast enough to react

Zachary Kingston’s presentation distinguished forgiving demonstrations from tasks in which time matters. In a nearly static setting, a robot may pause to reason or recover from a mistake. Intercepting a moving object or responding to a changing obstacle requires much faster decisions.

The examples used rapid motion planning for manipulators and higher-dimensional systems, including whole-body motion. The talk also described combining these planning tools with learned policies and vision-language-action models.

The key idea was to give a higher-level system tools that can respond at the necessary timescale. Model-based planning can then handle motion constraints while learned components contribute task understanding or other capabilities.

Understand policies and coordinate teams

The next research overview connected robot teaching, policy interpretation, safety constraints, and multi-agent learning. One direction examined internal features of vision-language-action policies to understand which representations affect task success, motion characteristics, and target selection.

Other examples involved steering behaviour with logical constraints, detecting undesirable coordination between agents, and enabling teams to follow strategies communicated through sketches. A multi-agent objective can produce unexpected collective behaviour, so understanding the team’s incentives matters alongside each agent’s individual performance.

Together, these examples treated human teaching, internal representations, and collective incentives as parts of understanding and shaping robot behaviour.

Use autonomous racing to test the whole stack

Autonomous racing provided a systems-level example of perception, planning, and control under tight physical limits. At high speed, even a short interval between sensor updates corresponds to a substantial distance travelled. Sensor fusion and prediction must therefore support decisions with very little delay.

Planning also needs to account for other teams’ behaviour and willingness to take risks. Control must translate the selected manoeuvre into feasible motion near the vehicle’s performance limits.

In the discussion, adaptation was described as a correction to an existing model. Changes in conditions, such as tyre temperature and available friction, can be handled through sensing and online adaptation without attempting to relearn the entire vehicle model from scratch on each lap.

Build visual models that answer at the right time

Raymond Yeh’s presentation connected computer vision to three needs of embodied AI: reconstructing environments, reasoning about observations, and maintaining robust perception.

The examples included recovering 3D scene structure from an image, building time-varying representations from video, and answering questions about spatial relationships. For a live video stream, a correct answer is not enough: the system also needs to determine when the relevant evidence has become available and respond promptly.

The presentation also showed how apparently minor visual changes can alter a model’s answer unexpectedly. This motivated work on robustness to transformations such as changes in object scale.

Will one large model be enough?

The panel did not reach a single answer about whether a general vision-language-action model should become the central component of a robot.

Some responses emphasized the ability of large models to absorb capabilities previously handled by specialized systems. Others argued for modular or hierarchical designs, especially when perception, reasoning, and control operate at different timescales. A model that can call a conventional planner also complicates the distinction between a single intelligent system and a collection of specialized components.

The practical questions were about latency, constraints, failure diagnosis, and choosing methods appropriate to the task. Several speakers emphasized that a plausible plan still needs a way to be checked before it becomes a physical action.

Scaling data and keeping humans involved

The data discussion covered teleoperation, human video, synthetic environments, and the use of physical priors. Speakers stressed that quantity, diversity, quality, and alignment with deployment conditions all matter.

A difficulty with indirect demonstrations is connecting what is visible in a video to the forces and actions needed by a particular robot. Precise contact tasks make that mismatch especially important. Coordinated demonstrations involving several people or robots introduce further collection challenges.

Human input also extends beyond initial demonstrations. Corrections, preferences, rewards, and sketches can help communicate a desired behaviour. The closing exchange raised an earlier problem in that process: people may struggle to articulate what they actually want, even before the system attempts to learn or execute it.

Safety remains a systems question

The safety discussion ranged from physical failures, such as a humanoid falling, to context-dependent requirements and how a person experiences an interaction. It also raised a difficult question: if a foundation model can itself fail unpredictably, using it to supervise another component does not automatically make the resulting system safe.

Across the session, the central deployment problem was connecting capabilities to explicit assumptions, checks, and mechanisms for responding when those assumptions no longer hold.

Source and related notes

The official session page lists the panelists and moderator. These notes summarize the recorded presentations and discussion; unclear project names and numerical claims without sufficient context are omitted.

Other sessions from the same event:

  • From AI Capabilities to Useful Tools
  • AI and Big Data for Transportation Systems
entry.summary: Lightning talks and a panel on physical grounding, reactive planning, interpretable policies, multi-robot coordination, and deployment safety.

entry.title: AI and Big Data for Transportation Systems

link.title: AI and Big Data for Transportation Systems

entry.content:
Session: AI and Big Data Innovations in Transportation System Management
Panelists: Darcy Bullock, Lyndsay Quist, and Seval Oz
Moderator: Eric Clark
Event: Purdue + Google AI Summit 2026
Date: October 29, 2026

The available recording captures part of a transportation panel discussing how AI and large datasets can support engineering decisions. It begins and ends mid-sentence, so these notes cover the recorded excerpt rather than the full session.

Validate measurements before modelling

The discussion emphasized that AI does not replace basic engineering and physical reasoning. Large volumes of measurements still need checks against the properties of the hardware, software, and physical system that produced them.

This matters when combining different data sources. Before interpreting a pattern, engineers need to understand what each measurement represents and how the collection methods might affect the result. More records alone do not establish that a model’s conclusion is reliable.

Feed vehicle data back into road design

Darcy Bullock discussed how vehicle measurements could help examine existing design practices, particularly in construction zones. The examples connected road roughness, lateral motion, acceleration, and possible indicators of crash risk.

The role described for AI was to help identify patterns and direct engineering attention toward locations or design choices worth investigating. Those patterns can then inform further investigation and feed back into the design process.

The panel also stressed learning across states and institutions. Sharing data and experience can help agencies compare approaches rather than treating every local deployment as an isolated experiment.

Be explicit about the safety objective

Another part of the discussion contrasted reducing the consequences of crashes with avoiding collisions. These objectives are related, but they call for different measurements and evaluation criteria.

For autonomous systems, the question is therefore broader than whether an algorithm performs well on one metric. Evaluation needs to connect the chosen metric to the intended safety outcome and to the conditions in which the system will operate.

Move toward demonstrations that test deployment conditions

The excerpt also discussed moving beyond limited pilots toward demonstrations that reveal whether a technology can operate at a useful scale. High-speed autonomous racing appeared as an example of a demanding environment for studying vehicle dynamics and rapid decisions.

The broader message was that engineering validation, institutional coordination, and deployment evidence need to develop alongside the AI methods themselves.

Source and related notes

The official session page provides the session name and participant list. Some speaker names and policy references are unclear in the recording; those uncertain details are not reconstructed here.

  • From AI Capabilities to Useful Tools
  • Robotics and Embodied AI: From Demos to Deployment

entry.title: From AI Capabilities to Useful Tools

link.title: From AI Capabilities to Useful Tools

entry.content:
Speaker: Charles Elliott, Google Labs
Event: Purdue + Google AI Summit 2026
Date: October 29, 2026

Charles Elliott’s keynote examined what it takes to turn improving AI capabilities into useful products. The emphasis was on choosing worthwhile problems, understanding how people work, and giving agents enough context and oversight to make progress over longer periods.

Start with a problem worth solving

Elliott described Google Labs and Google X as environments for exploring ideas that may not yet fit an established product. A recurring principle was to stay committed to the underlying problem while remaining willing to change the proposed solution.

He also argued for revisiting ideas that were previously impractical. A task may become feasible as models improve, costs fall, or the right expertise becomes available. An earlier unsuccessful prototype therefore does not necessarily settle whether an idea is worth pursuing.

One example came from laboratory automation: using models to help translate experimental protocols into code for laboratory robots. The broader point was that useful applications often connect disciplines, requiring both technical capability and an understanding of the domain in which a tool will be used.

Design around the user’s work

The talk used taste to describe judgment about what makes an AI tool helpful in a particular setting. For a developer, this might involve the interface and workflow. For a researcher, it might concern how scientific material is explained or how a proposed method fits an existing process.

Examples included notebook-style assistants that turn source material into accessible explanations and audio discussions, and creative tools developed with input from filmmakers and other creators. These examples illustrated why the surrounding tool matters: users need ways to supply context, steer the output, and continue working with it.

Elliott also distinguished producing a technically valid artifact from communicating it well. A formal proof or lengthy research document may still be difficult for a person to understand. Presentation and interpretability remain part of making the output useful.

Give long-running agents a clear objective

The next theme was the friction of repeatedly correcting or redirecting an assistant. Agents that operate for hours need a stronger understanding of the user’s intentions than a short prompt may provide.

Elliott described an interview-style interaction in which an agent asks questions about the task before beginning. This can help users express goals they understand intuitively but have not yet specified clearly. Clarifying the objective early may reduce unnecessary work and repeated intervention later.

He discussed research workflows involving literature exploration, hypothesis generation, and computational searches for improvements to existing algorithms. Across these examples, the agent needs both an objective and evidence against which to assess its progress.

Use agents to generate and challenge hypotheses

The co-scientist example organized hypothesis generation as a process of proposing, reviewing, comparing, and refining ideas. Different agents can bring different perspectives or tools, such as access to literature or computational environments. Tournament-style comparisons and Elo-style ratings help prioritize candidates.

The surrounding workflow starts with selecting a problem, gathering relevant data, and defining an analysis strategy. The proposed hypotheses then give the researcher concrete candidates to investigate.

Increase autonomy with checkpoints

Elliott closed by connecting autonomy to permissions, cost, and confidence in the result. The suggested progression involved bounded environments for exploration, opportunities for human review, and greater independence only where the work can be evaluated adequately.

His distinction between generating code and accepting it into a codebase was especially concrete: a large amount of AI-generated output does not remove the need for review, evaluation, and benchmarks. The same distinction applies to agents producing research artifacts over longer runs.

Source and related notes

These notes summarize the recorded keynote. Unclear phrases and an untranscribed video segment are omitted. The official summit agenda identifies the speaker and session date.

Other sessions from the same event:

  • AI and Big Data for Transportation Systems
  • Robotics and Embodied AI: From Demos to Deployment
entry.summary: Charles Elliott’s keynote on product judgment, scientific workflows, and oversight for long-running AI agents.

entry.title: Identifying Discrete-State Network Dynamics
entry.content:
Speaker: Carolyn L. Beck, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Date: October 23, 2026
Series: Purdue ICON Weekly Seminar / ECE Distinguished Lecture

The lecture asked how to identify a networked dynamical system when its observed states take only discrete values. The main goal was to recover network weights and topology from binary time series, with guarantees on the estimation error after a finite number of observations.

These notes are based on two partial transcripts and four slide screenshots. A middle segment was not recorded, so the summary covers the available material without reconstructing the missing discussion.

From binary observations to network structure

Examples included opinion dynamics, epidemic spread, gene regulation, and cascading defaults in financial networks. In each case, a node’s state can depend on its neighbors’ earlier states. The identification problem is to infer those interactions from the observed evolution of the network.

For a network with $p$ binary nodes, the full state space has $2^p$ elements. Estimating an unrestricted Markov transition matrix therefore involves exponentially many entries. The lecture instead used a Bernoulli autoregressive (BAR) model, which expresses each node’s activation probability through a weighted combination of the previous network state and a noise contribution.

After combining the noise parameters into an offset, the conditional activation probability has the form

\[\Pr\!\left(X_i(k+1)=1\mid X(k)\right) =a_i^{\mathsf T}X(k)+c_i.\]

Here, $a_i$ contains the incoming network weights for node $i$. Together, the weight matrix and offsets have $p^2+p$ parameters. Parameter constraints keep the probabilities valid. In the basic nonnegative-influence model, persistent noise prevents the process from remaining trapped at an all-zero or all-one state and supports identification.

This is a structured model of the transition dynamics: the reduction in parameters comes from the BAR assumptions, rather than from an ability to estimate any arbitrary Markov chain with the same amount of data.

Consistency and the two estimators

The talk distinguished strong consistency from sample complexity. Consistency asks whether an estimator converges to the true parameters as the observation horizon grows without bound. Sample complexity asks how many observations suffice for a specified error with high probability.

The lecture considered the direct maximum likelihood estimator and a closed-form estimator. Empirical state and transition counts supply estimates of conditional probabilities; the BAR structure then relates these probabilities to the network parameters through linear equations. The displayed closed-form construction uses a Gram-matrix inverse.

The finite-sample analysis presented later concerned the closed-form estimator. The speaker identified corresponding sample-complexity guarantees for the direct maximum likelihood estimator as an open problem.

What controls the number of observations?

One slide gave a sufficient sample-size requirement on the scale

\[\frac{p^3\log p} {(1-r)^2\epsilon^2\lambda_{\min}(\Pi)^2}\]

to obtain $\lVert\widehat{\Theta}-\Theta_0\rVert_F<\epsilon$ with high probability, under the stated model assumptions. The quantities have distinct roles:

  • Network dimension $p$: larger networks require more observations.
  • Target error $\epsilon$: a smaller error tolerance increases the sample requirement.
  • Dobrushin coefficient $r$: this describes dependence and contraction of the process. As $r$ approaches one, the dependence makes the bound less favorable.
  • Correlation matrix $\Pi$: this is the second-moment matrix of the state augmented with a constant. A small minimum eigenvalue indicates poor conditioning for parameter estimation.

The interpretation of $r$ was how quickly the process forgets its earlier conditions. This matters because consecutive observations are dependent; a long trajectory cannot simply be treated as equally many independent samples.

The requirement is a conservative sufficient condition, obtained by bounding the estimation error. It does not establish a matching lower bound on the number of samples every estimator must use. This distinction also came up in the questions after the talk.

How the proof separates the difficulties

The slides bounded the spectral-norm estimation error by a ratio: a random error term in the numerator and the minimum eigenvalue of a data Gram matrix in the denominator. The proof therefore needs an upper bound on the numerator and a positive lower bound on the denominator, both holding with high probability.

For the denominator, the argument rescales the data matrix using its expected second moments and controls how far the resulting Gram matrix deviates from the identity. Since the observations form a dependent process, this requires concentration results for Markov chains rather than a direct independent-sample argument.

For the numerator, the slides used a matrix Freedman inequality. The error can be expressed through a martingale difference sequence, allowing matrix concentration bounds to control it. Combining the two estimates yields the finite-sample guarantee.

Applications and open directions

The reported simulations suggested that the theoretical sample requirement could be conservative. Gene-signaling examples also involved positive and negative influences. More recent work explored dependencies in waterway transportation networks, including seasonal usage of locks.

The lecture closed with several directions for further work: tighter bounds, guarantees for the direct likelihood estimator, and the use of known network structure. For example, physical geography can rule out particular connections in a waterway network. Such information, or assumptions about sparsity and maximum degree, could reduce the identification burden.

Other extensions included partial observation, states with more than two values, and alternative estimators. The presentation’s main analysis assumed that all node states were observed over time.

Related paper

Xiaotian Xie, Dimitrios Katselis, Carolyn L. Beck, and R. Srikant. Finite Sample Analysis for Structured Discrete System Identification. IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 68(10), 6345–6352, 2023. The paper gives the formal assumptions and results behind the finite-sample analysis.
entry.summary: ICON seminar notes on Bernoulli autoregressive models, network identification, and finite-sample estimation guarantees.

entry.title: Learning Causal Graphs with Mixed-Integer Optimization

link.title: Learning Causal Graphs with Mixed-Integer Optimization

entry.content:
Speaker: Simge Küçükyavuz, Northwestern University
Date: October 16, 2026
Series: Optimization seminar, Purdue University

The seminar discussed how optimization can help learn directed graphical models from observational data. The main setting was a linear Gaussian structural equation model, with particular attention to the case where different variables have different noise variances. The talk connected three ideas: a convex mixed-integer formulation, an early stopping rule guided by statistical accuracy, and a coordinate descent method for larger problems.

Learning a graph from data

The opening example involved exercise, body weight, and heart health. Observations may reveal relationships among these variables, but learning a directed graph requires deciding which relationships exist and how they are oriented. The model considered in the talk represents these relationships with a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

Each variable is expressed as a linear combination of its parents plus a noise term. Learning the model therefore means estimating both the graph structure and the coefficients on its edges. The objective combines a negative log-likelihood with an L0 penalty, which counts nonzero edge coefficients and encourages a sparse graph. An acyclicity constraint rules out directed cycles.

A key distinction was between equal and unequal noise variances. Equal variances can make the graph identifiable under suitable assumptions. With unequal variances, observational data generally cannot determine every edge direction uniquely. The appropriate target is then a Markov equivalence class: a collection of DAGs that encode the same conditional independencies. A completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) represents this class, showing which directions are shared across its members and which remain unresolved.

A convex mixed-integer formulation

The original likelihood formulation contains difficult interactions between the edge coefficients and noise variances. The speaker described a change of variables based on a factorization of the precision matrix, the inverse covariance matrix.

The DAG structure is useful here: there exists a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns that makes the relevant matrix triangular. This allows a log-determinant expression to be rewritten using scalar logarithms of diagonal entries. The resulting formulation has a convex continuous objective, together with discrete decisions that encode the graph.

Binary variables indicate whether edges are present. They also make it possible to count edges for the L0 penalty. Layer variables enforce acyclicity by requiring a selected edge to move forward in the layer ordering. The formulation can incorporate a candidate superstructure to restrict the search, as well as prior knowledge about particular relationships. The talk also mentioned perspective strengthening as a way to improve continuous relaxations.

Stopping at a statistically meaningful accuracy

Branch and bound maintains a lower bound from relaxations and an upper bound from feasible solutions. Their difference measures the remaining optimization gap. Finding a good graph may be much faster than proving that no better graph exists.

The seminar connected this gap to the statistical properties of the estimator. Under the stated assumptions, an appropriately chosen stopping threshold can preserve consistency without requiring the solver to close the gap completely. The threshold depends on statistical quantities such as regularization and sparsity.

The experiments illustrated the tradeoff: a suitable early stopping rule reduced computation while maintaining estimation quality, whereas stopping with too large a gap could reduce accuracy. A practical complication discussed in the questions was that the true graph sparsity is unknown and must be estimated when applying the rule.

Coordinate descent for larger problems

For larger graphs, the talk introduced a coordinate descent algorithm. It updates one entry of the transformed parameter matrix at a time while keeping the others fixed. An update that would create a directed cycle is excluded.

The method has convergence guarantees to a coordinate-wise minimum. Under the paper’s assumptions, its objective value also approaches the optimal penalized likelihood value as the sample size grows, with finite-sample statistical guarantees. This asymptotic result does not imply that every finite-data run finds a globally optimal solution.

The reported experiments compared computation time and differences between estimated and true CPDAGs. They showed the benefits of accounting for unequal noise variances and the speed of coordinate descent on larger benchmark networks. The discussion also highlighted the importance of the coordinate update order.

Further discussion

The closing discussion covered using expert knowledge or interventions to resolve ambiguous directions, extending the model beyond the linear Gaussian setting, and exploiting structure in sparse quadratic optimization problems. One computational distinction was that the data enter the formulation through a sample covariance matrix: increasing the sample size does not directly add graph-decision variables, while increasing the number of nodes or candidate edges expands the combinatorial search.

Related papers

These notes summarize the seminar rather than reproduce its proofs. The following papers provide the precise assumptions and guarantees behind the two main methods:

  • Tong Xu, Armeen Taeb, Simge Küçükyavuz, and Ali Shojaie. Integer programming for learning directed acyclic graphs from nonidentifiable Gaussian models. Biometrika, 2025.
  • Tong Xu, Simge Küçükyavuz, Ali Shojaie, and Armeen Taeb. An Asymptotically Optimal Coordinate Descent Algorithm for Learning Bayesian Networks from Gaussian Models.
